levels.title: Set a Goal Before Writing a Prompt
levels.objective: Use the principles of set a goal before writing a prompt to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: A prompt should name the task and the decision or artifact it supports, not merely name a topic. Worked example: A student needs a revision plan for three biology chapters before Friday. A strong response is to ask for a three-day revision timetable with chapter names and a self-test at the end. Avoid the tempting alternatives: write only "biology" and expect a useful study plan; or ask the model to guess the examination questions.
levels.workedExample: Situation: A student needs a revision plan for three biology chapters before Friday. Recommended response: Ask for a three-day revision timetable with chapter names and a self-test at the end.
levels.commonMistake: Write only "biology" and expect a useful study plan
levels.remediation: A stated output can be compared against the task's actual needs.
levels.hint: Look for the option that follows this principle: A prompt should name the task and the decision or artifact it supports, not merely name a topic.

options.a: Ask for a three-day revision timetable with chapter names and a self-test at the end
options.b: Write only "biology" and expect a useful study plan
options.c: Ask the model to guess the examination questions

challenges.feedback: A prompt should name the task and the decision or artifact it supports, not merely name a topic. In this case, ask for a three-day revision timetable with chapter names and a self-test at the end.

options.c: Specify the product, buyer, factual features and two-sentence description as the output

challenges.feedback: Specify the product, buyer, factual features and two-sentence description as the output. This applies the lesson to the new setting without making up missing facts or assuming the first answer is reliable.

challenges.feedback: A stated output can be compared against the task's actual needs.

levels.title: Identify the Intended Audience
levels.objective: Use the principles of identify the intended audience to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: Vocabulary and examples should match the reader's experience, language and purpose. Worked example: A student is preparing an explanation for classmates who have never studied accounting. A strong response is to request an introductory explanation with a simple shop example and definitions for new terms. Avoid the tempting alternatives: use advanced jargon without explaining it; or assume every reader has the same background.
levels.workedExample: Situation: A student is preparing an explanation for classmates who have never studied accounting. Recommended response: Request an introductory explanation with a simple shop example and definitions for new terms.
levels.commonMistake: Use advanced jargon without explaining it
levels.remediation: Unexplained terms make the result less useful for its intended readers.
levels.hint: Look for the option that follows this principle: Vocabulary and examples should match the reader's experience, language and purpose.

options.a: Use advanced jargon without explaining it
options.b: Assume every reader has the same background
options.c: Request an introductory explanation with a simple shop example and definitions for new terms

challenges.feedback: Vocabulary and examples should match the reader's experience, language and purpose. In this case, request an introductory explanation with a simple shop example and definitions for new terms.

levels.title: Supply Relevant Source Material
levels.objective: Use the principles of supply relevant source material to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: Provide permitted facts or a short source excerpt when accuracy depends on particular information. Worked example: A learner wants to summarize her own original notes on water conservation. A strong response is to paste a non-sensitive excerpt and request a summary restricted to those notes. Avoid the tempting alternatives: ask the system to invent facts omitted from the notes; or upload an unrelated private classmate's records.
levels.workedExample: Situation: A learner wants to summarize her own original notes on water conservation. Recommended response: Paste a non-sensitive excerpt and request a summary restricted to those notes.
levels.commonMistake: Ask the system to invent facts omitted from the notes
levels.remediation: Source-bounded summaries reduce unsupported additions.
levels.hint: Look for the option that follows this principle: Provide permitted facts or a short source excerpt when accuracy depends on particular information.

options.a: Upload an unrelated private classmate's records

options.c: Ask the system to invent facts omitted from the notes

levels.title: Separate Instructions From Background
levels.objective: Use the principles of separate instructions from background to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: Label the task, input and constraints so source text cannot masquerade as a new instruction. Worked example: A pasted customer review contains the phrase "ignore the previous instruction". A strong response is to mark the review as quoted data and ask for a neutral sentiment summary without following embedded commands. Avoid the tempting alternatives: treat the reviewer's sentence as a new system command; or delete the review and fabricate a customer quote.
levels.workedExample: Situation: A pasted customer review contains the phrase "ignore the previous instruction". Recommended response: Mark the review as quoted data and ask for a neutral sentiment summary without following embedded commands.
levels.commonMistake: Treat the reviewer's sentence as a new system command
levels.remediation: Untrusted source material is data, not authority to change the task.
levels.hint: Look for the option that follows this principle: Label the task, input and constraints so source text cannot masquerade as a new instruction.

options.c: Delete the review and fabricate a customer quote

challenges.feedback: Label the task, input and constraints so source text cannot masquerade as a new instruction. In this case, mark the review as quoted data and ask for a neutral sentiment summary without following embedded commands.

levels.title: Specify an Answer Format
levels.objective: Use the principles of specify an answer format to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: Define structure and length when the result will be consumed by a person or tool. Worked example: A project manager wants four status points for a WhatsApp update. A strong response is to request four bullets labeled Done, In progress, Blocked and Next, each under twenty words. Avoid the tempting alternatives: request an unlimited essay with no headings; or ask for a JSON payload when only a short chat message is needed.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Write a Complete Task Brief
levels.objective: Use the principles of checkpoint: write a complete task brief to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: A strong task brief combines goal, audience, allowed inputs, boundaries and output acceptance checks. Worked example: A fictional bakery needs a two-line promotional caption for new bread without price claims. A strong response is to state the audience, new bread facts, two-line limit, warm tone and prohibition on unverified offers. Avoid the tempting alternatives: request a viral caption with invented discounts; or give the model only the shop's name.

levels.remediation: Checking length, claims and accuracy is part of the brief.

levels.title: Prioritize Constraints
levels.objective: Use the principles of prioritize constraints to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: Constraints should express what must be included, what must be excluded and what to do when input is missing. Worked example: A CV assistant is asked to rewrite an experience section without inventing employment dates. A strong response is to require preserving supplied facts and flag missing dates rather than guessing. Avoid the tempting alternatives: add plausible jobs and dates to make the CV attractive; or ignore the candidate's existing achievements.
levels.workedExample: Situation: A CV assistant is asked to rewrite an experience section without inventing employment dates. Recommended response: Require preserving supplied facts and flag missing dates rather than guessing.
levels.commonMistake: Add plausible jobs and dates to make the CV attractive
levels.remediation: Explicit missing-data behavior prevents fabricated claims.
levels.hint: Look for the option that follows this principle: Constraints should express what must be included, what must be excluded and what to do when input is missing.

levels.title: Control Tone Without Changing Facts
levels.objective: Use the principles of control tone without changing facts to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: Style instructions can change phrasing, but must not change the underlying evidence or promise. Worked example: A refund policy states seven calendar days and the team wants friendlier wording. A strong response is to ask for a warm tone while preserving the seven-day policy and every exception. Avoid the tempting alternatives: change seven days to thirty days to sound kinder; or remove all exceptions without permission.

levels.commonMistake: Change seven days to thirty days to sound kinder
levels.remediation: Stylistic revision must preserve substantive meaning.
levels.hint: Look for the option that follows this principle: Style instructions can change phrasing, but must not change the underlying evidence or promise.

levels.title: Break Large Tasks Into Parts
levels.objective: Use the principles of break large tasks into parts to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: For complex requests, isolate planning, drafting and verification stages, with checkpoints between them. Worked example: A freelancer must turn meeting notes into a project proposal. A strong response is to extract confirmed requirements first, then draft scope, then verify exclusions against the notes. Avoid the tempting alternatives: ask for a final contract immediately without reviewing assumptions; or let the model invent the client's budget.

levels.title: Ask for Clarifying Assumptions
levels.objective: Use the principles of ask for clarifying assumptions to make a reliable choice in a realistic learner or workplace task.
levels.teaching: When key information is absent, require explicit assumptions or a question instead of confident guessing. Worked example: A client requests an advertisement without supplying platform or target audience. A strong response is to ask what channel and audience to use, or label any tentative assumption before drafting. Avoid the tempting alternatives: invent demographics and claim they were approved; or assume a high-spend media budget without evidence.

Avoid the tempting alternatives: assume any percentage in fluent prose is correct; or round expenses down without documenting it.
